core.title: Parameterise SQL; never interpolate or concatenate it
core.given: Code calls a query sink (a call that executes SQL; which calls count is stack data from the profile)
core.when: SQL text is passed to that sink
core.then: Do not build that SQL by string interpolation or concatenation; parameterise it — pass each value as a bound parameter through the stack's parameterising form, never spliced into the SQL text.
prefer: Write the SQL as a static statement with placeholders and bind each value as a parameter.
Where the stack provides a form that binds every substitution as a parameter by construction, build the whole statement with it.
avoid: Splicing a value into the SQL text by interpolation before the sink sees it.
Concatenating a SQL string with a value.
Mistaking a plain interpolated string for the stack's parameterising form; the two can look almost identical.
unless: SQL passed through a form that parameterises each substitution by construction is parameterised and is never flagged.

An interpolation-assembled statement containing no SQL keyword is not SQL and is skipped; this keyword skip scopes only the interpolation check — the concatenation check has no such exemption and applies independently.
Static SQL with no interpolation is not injectable.
core.why: A parameterising form binds each value as a parameter; interpolation or concatenation produces a finished SQL string before the sink sees it, so the values become part of the SQL.
evidence: The stack's SQL-injection check reports no finding on the touched files (a finding is verification evidence, not a precondition for applying the rule).

Reviewer confirms every query-sink call touched passes either static SQL with no interpolation or concatenation, placeholders with bound parameters, or a form that parameterises each substitution by construction.
verification: The check has two independent branches and flags a query-sink call when either fires: SQL text assembled by interpolation (a value spliced into the statement text), or a SQL string concatenated with another value. The concrete syntactic shapes are recognised by the realization in the stack's syntax.

The check skips: SQL passed through a form that parameterises each substitution by construction; interpolation-assembled statements containing no SQL keyword; and static SQL with no interpolation or concatenation. The keyword skip belongs to the interpolation branch only — it never suppresses the concatenation branch, which applies independently of it.

A form that parameterises each substitution is safe by construction yet can be visually almost identical to the unsafe plain form; the check flags only the unsafe form. This distinction is load-bearing.
Severity 4; disposition strict (declared by the rule, not the profile).

The change signal (SQL text passed to a query sink) is a scope signal, not an exclusive gate: it applies to any such call — new, edited, or existing being worked on. A realization gates conjunctively on stack membership (profile data), the languages of its in-scope files (profile data), and this change signal.

fires: A query sink receives SQL text assembled by interpolating a value into a statement with a SQL keyword.
A query sink receives SQL text built by concatenating a SQL string with a value.
SQL text assembled by interpolation or concatenation is passed to the stack's parameterising mechanism as a plain string instead of through its binding form.
Any of these shapes appears in a test file (any test role) or in an existing query-sink call being touched, not only in newly written code.
doesNotFire: SQL is passed through the stack's binding form that parameterises each substitution by construction.
An interpolation-assembled statement containing no SQL keyword (not SQL); the keyword test never suppresses the concatenation branch, which applies independently.
A query sink called with a placeholder statement plus bound parameter values.
The same call shape in a project that does not belong to this stack; this realization does not scope it.

bunOnly.text: bun_security_hygiene_detector reports no SECURITY-SQL-INJECTION-001 finding on the touched files.
bunOnly.reason: Detector and finding ids of this one rule are realization details; the core names the check generically.

bunOnly.text: Template literals with no SQL keyword are not SQL and are skipped — the exception's syntactic carrier in Bun is the (untagged) template literal; the detector's keyword test applies only to the template-literal branch, never to the quoted-string concatenation branch.
bunOnly.reason: The exception's applicability is syntactic: Bun exempts only the interpolation shape (template literals), and its concatenation branch has no such exemption. The neutral core keeps the exception scoped to interpolation-assembled statements and states that the concatenation check applies independently; naming the template-literal shape itself is this stack's syntax.

bunOnly.text: Flag a query-sink call whose first argument is a template literal containing both a SQL keyword and a ${} interpolation, or a quoted SQL string followed by +.
bunOnly.reason: The concrete syntactic shapes (first-argument template literal, ${} interpolation, + concatenation, and the keyword test sitting only in the template-literal branch) are this stack's syntax as encoded in its detector; the neutral core states the check as two independent branches — interpolated SQL (keyword-gated) and concatenated SQL — with the keyword skip scoped to the interpolation branch.

bunOnly.text: Term tagged_template: sql`…` — a template invoking a function that PARAMETERISES each substitution; safe by construction and visually almost identical to the untagged form that is not; the detector therefore flags only the untagged shape.
bunOnly.reason: The named Bun construct (the tagged sql template) has no neutral name; the neutral distinction (binding by construction vs plain string building) lives in core verification, and the construct itself is carried as profile data (idiom.sql_parameterisation).

neutralityNotes: The obligation itself (never build SQL by interpolation or concatenation; bind values as parameters) is fully neutral. What could not be neutralized: (1) the load-bearing tagged-vs-untagged template distinction is the Bun instance of a neutral distinction (a form that binds every substitution by construction vs plain string building); the neutral distinction is kept in core (verification, why, avoid[2], unless[0]) while the named construct is profile data (proposed idiom.sql_parameterisation) and the detector's syntactic shapes are bunOnly. (2) The no-keyword skip is syntactic in Bun — it exempts only template literals, and the quoted-string concatenation branch has no such exemption; the neutral core therefore scopes the skip to interpolation-assembled statements and states in unless[1], verification[1] and doesNotFire that the concatenation branch applies independently of it, with the template-literal shape itself retained in the realization (bunOnly unless[1]). (3) Stack-membership and language gates have no closed neutral activation-fact kind (the fact vocabulary offers role/operation/change/phase/finding/file_kind/task_term/task_has_acceptance), so they are carried as profile data (proposed tooling.stack_signals; proposed tooling.in_scope_languages — the latter because tooling.languages documents production-source languages only, while the Bun gate covers source and test files alike) plus a bunOnly entry for the Bun observer; the core keeps only the change fact and states the conjunctive gating in verification. (4) Detector, validator and finding ids, and the concrete first-argument/`${}`/`+` flag shapes, remain bunOnly per the notProfileKeys rule; severity 4 and strict disposition stay in core:verification. Instantiating the core with the Bun profile values and the bunOnly items reproduces bun.json's scope and obligation exactly — no exception dropped (the keyword skip keeps its template-literal-only reach), no condition added.
